lektion.einfuehrung.kurz: What React is – in simple words.
lektion.einfuehrung.aufgabe: Switch the language (DE/EN) in the top right and watch the whole page change. That is exactly what React does: when the data changes, the view updates on its own.
lektion.projekt.kurz: How this learning path is built and how it works.
lektion.komponenten.kurz: What a component is and what JSX looks like.
lektion.komponenten.aufgabe: Open src/lessons/Lesson_ComponentsJSX.tsx and change the text in the `name` variable from "Welt" to your own name. Save – the browser refreshes on its own.
lektion.props.aufgabe: In src/lessons/Lesson_Props.tsx: pass a different name to one <Greeting />. Then add a fourth <Greeting /> with a new name and a `mood` of your choice.
lektion.state.aufgabe: In src/lessons/Lesson_State.tsx: change the starting value in useState(0) to 10. Then add a third button 'Reset' that sets the number back to 0 with setCount(0).

lektion.events.aufgabe: In src/lessons/Lesson_Events.tsx: also show the entered text in UPPERCASE. Hint: text.toUpperCase() turns a text into upper case.
lektion.i18n.kurz: How the DE/EN switch works – and how to extend it.
lektion.i18n.aufgabe:
1) Open src/i18n/en.json and change the value of "app.untertitel" to a sentence of your own. Save and watch the page header.
2) Add the SAME new key "app.fusszeile" to BOTH files (de.json AND en.json) – with a German and an English text. Then show it somewhere with t("app.fusszeile").
3) For the brave: add a THIRD language. Copy de.json to fr.json, translate a few values and register the language in LanguageContext.tsx (in the `Language` type and the `dictionaries` object) as well as in the LanguageSwitcher.
lektion.roadmap.kurz: What you need to join an existing React project.
lektion.roadmap.aufgabe: Practise reading unfamiliar code: use your editor's search to find every place useState appears in this project. For each hit, answer: What does this state remember? Who changes it? That is exactly how you approach any existing React project.
lektion.agintro.kurz: How an agent system fundamentally works.
lektion.agintro.aufgabe: Open the .github/ folder in this project. Find out: which agent would be responsible for a CSS change – and which instructions file would automatically be loaded along with it? (Hint: look into agents/project.agent.md and instructions/styles.instructions.md.)
lektion.agsim.kurz: This repo's Copilot setup – try it out interactively.
lektion.agsim.aufgabe:
1) Play through all five tasks in the simulator and toggle the three mechanisms off and on one by one. Watch how costs and warnings change.
2) Practice: open Copilot Chat in VS Code, pick the 'project' agent and ask it for a small change. Compare its behaviour with the simulator.
3) For the brave: add a fourth specialist in .github/agents/ (e.g. 'tests') and extend the decision table in the project agent.
einf.p1: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces – everything you see on the screen. The key idea: you build the interface out of many small, reusable building blocks called components.
einf.p2: The clever part: you describe WHAT should be shown – not step by step HOW. When your data changes, React automatically makes the screen match it. You never update the interface by hand.
einf.p3: An app comes together like Lego bricks: many small components are plugged together into a whole page. This learning path itself is built exactly that way.
einf.beispiel.hinweis: This little example runs live in React:
proj.p1: This app IS your tutorial. On the left you see the list of all lessons, on the right the selected one – with a short explanation, a runnable live example and (usually) a small task.
proj.p2: Use Back / Next or click in the list to switch lessons. Switching runs purely through a state value (useState) on purpose – no router yet. A router comes as a later step.
proj.p3: Each lesson is its own file under src/lessons/. To add a new one, create a file and register it once in src/lessons/lessons.ts. That's all it takes.
proj.p4: Tip: open the files in src/ while you read. Each starts with a short comment "Was macht diese Datei?" (what does this file do?) – first in German, then in English right below – and also explains the TypeScript specifics.
proj.p5: Note: the names in the code (files, components, variables) are English – just like in most real projects. The German understanding comes from the comments right next to them.
proj.zaehlung: This learning path currently contains {count} lessons.
proj.spiel.p1: You can NOT permanently break anything here. The project is a Git repository: a single command (git restore .) resets all files to the last clean state. So experiment boldly!
proj.spiel.p2: If you introduce an error while experimenting, the browser shows a red error message (Vite's "error overlay"). That is not a crash but a hint: fix the file, save – and the app immediately keeps running.
proj.spiel.p3: A good trick for practising: copy a lesson file, give the copy a new name and play around inside it. The original stays untouched.
mehr.p1: "i18n" is the common abbreviation for internationalization (i + 18 letters + n). It means: the app can run in several languages.
mehr.p2: The trick: the texts are NOT hard-coded in the components, but live in JSON files – here src/i18n/de.json and src/i18n/en.json. Both share the same keys, but with different values.
mehr.p3: A component asks for a text by its key: t("nav.weiter"). Depending on the chosen language, the t() function looks the value up in the matching JSON file.
mehr.p4: So that every component knows the current language, it is stored centrally in a React context (src/i18n/LanguageContext.tsx). The switch in the top right changes that single value – and the whole page re-renders.
mehr.p5: This text, too, comes from the JSON files. Switch between DE and EN above – it changes along.
l1.p1: This is your first component. Everything you see comes out of the function Lesson_ComponentsJSX.
l1.p2: In JSX you can insert JavaScript at any time using curly braces. Example: 2 + 3 =
l3.p1: Every click changes the state. Because the state changes, React re-renders the component – and the number above is correct again.
road.p1: In an existing React project you keep meeting the same building blocks. This list shows you what you already learn here, what comes next – and what additionally matters in day-to-day project work.
road.p2: Work through the groups in order. You don't have to master everything at once: once you understand group 1, you can already read along meaningfully and make small changes.
road.g1.h: 1) You learn this in this learning path
road.g1.i1: Components & JSX – the building blocks of every React app (lesson 5).
road.g1.i2: Props – passing data from parent to child component (lesson 6).
road.g1.i4: Lists with .map() and key – how a data array becomes a list on screen (lesson 10).
road.g1.i5: Conditional rendering – showing something only when a condition holds (lesson 9).
road.g1.i6: Context – providing values to the whole app without passing them through every level (lesson 13 – that is exactly how the language switch works!).
road.g1.i7: Shared state (lifting state up) – state moves to the shared parent component (lesson 11).
road.g2.i1: useRef & DOM access – direct references to elements, e.g. to focus an input field.
road.g2.i2: Custom hooks – moving recurring logic into a function useXyz().
road.g2.i3: Router – several pages with their own URLs (e.g. react-router).
road.g2.i4: Data from a server – fetch, loading states, error handling; in big projects often with TanStack Query.
road.g2.i5: Forms – several input fields, validation, submitting.
road.g2.i6: Bigger state – when context is enough and when tools like Zustand or Redux help.
road.g3.h: 3) Day-to-day work in an existing project
road.g3.i1: Understanding the tools – npm, package.json, node_modules and Vite: what really happens on start.
road.g3.i2: React DevTools – a browser extension to inspect the component tree, props and state live.
road.g3.i3: Reading unfamiliar code – start at the entry point (main.tsx) and follow the component tree downwards.
road.g3.i4: Everyday Git – branches, small commits, fearless experimenting and resetting.
road.g3.i5: Tests – checking with Vitest and Testing Library that components do what they should.
road.g3.i6: The official docs react.dev/learn – the best source for looking things up and going deeper.
agi.p1: An agent is a language model in a loop: it reads the task, uses tools (read files, edit, run commands), inspects the result – and continues until the task is done. Instructions (rules) steer its behaviour along the way.
agi.beispiel: Concretely: you tell GitHub Copilot in VS Code 'Rename the back button to Back to overview'. The agent finds the right file, changes the text, checks the result – and only then replies. This loop of reading, acting and checking is what turns a chat model into an agent.
agi.p2: Everything the model 'sees' – rules, code, intermediate steps – lands in its context window and costs tokens. Tokens are the little chunks of text models read and write – billing is per chunk, so they mean money and attention. The most important design rule is therefore: load as little as possible, as much as needed.
agi.p3: An agent SYSTEM is therefore not a single know-it-all but a team: a cheap router agent understands the task and passes it to the right specialist – with the right model (cheap for simple things, strong for tricky ones) and only the necessary tools.
agi.p4: There are five mechanisms for this, each with its own purpose:
agi.m1: Always-on instructions (copilot-instructions.md) – the project's iron rules. Loaded on EVERY request → keep them as short as humanly possible.
agi.m2: applyTo instructions (instructions/*.instructions.md) – rules for specific file areas. Loaded ONLY when matching files are touched.
agi.m3: Agents (agents/*.agent.md) – job profiles: model + tools + focus. The router delegates to them – but you can also select them directly in the chat at any time. With no agent selected, the model from the VS Code model picker applies.
agi.m4: Skills (skills/*/SKILL.md) – step-by-step procedures on demand. Only the short description is always visible; the content is loaded only when the procedure is actually needed.
agi.m5: Prompt files (prompts/*.prompt.md) – saved request templates for recurring asks, invoked in chat via /name (e.g. /new-lesson). Handy when many people on a team ask for the same thing often.
agi.merksatz: Mnemonic: instructions say HOW to behave. Agents decide WHO works (model + tools). Skills describe HOW a procedure runs. Prompt files store RECURRING requests as templates. And everything is loaded as rarely and as late as possible.
agi.transfer: For advanced readers: the pattern is tool-independent. Whether GitHub Copilot (.github/), Cursor (rules) or the AGENTS.md standard – the same scarce-context-budget principle applies everywhere. Once you understand it, you can set up any of these systems sensibly.
agi.sprache: By the way: the files under .github/ are deliberately single-language (English) and terse – they are handed to the model on every request, every line costs. The bilingual explanation lives here in the app and in the README.
modi.h: And if I pick no custom agent at all?
modi.p1: Then you work in one of the BUILT-IN modes you select in the Copilot picker. They are universal – but not tailored to your project:
modi.sp.name: Mode
modi.ask.tut: Asking & explaining. Answers, explains code, suggests changes – but does not edit or run anything itself.
modi.agent.tut: Gets tasks done autonomously: reads the codebase, edits several files, runs commands – in a loop until finished.
modi.agent.mod: from the picker – not fixed (maybe too expensive or too weak)
modi.plan.tut: Produces a step plan first instead of diving in. Good for bigger tasks, to avoid wrong turns.
modi.plan.kost: medium (an extra thinking step, but saves failed attempts)
modi.custom.name: Custom agent
modi.custom.tut: A pre-configured agent mode: fixed model, narrow tools, focused instructions. The router delegates to the fitting one.
modi.custom.werk: only the necessary ones (set per role)
modi.custom.kost: predictable & fitting (never needlessly expensive, never too weak)
modi.p2: The key is not 'cheaper' but FIXED: a custom agent deliberately sets the model (fitting – neither too expensive nor too weak), the tools (only the necessary ones) and the focus. With the built-in modes all of that depends on the picker – which can turn out too expensive or too weak. For a quick question ask mode is plenty; for recurring project work the custom agent delivers predictable, fitting results. Still important: the rules from copilot-instructions.md and the applyTo instructions apply in ALL modes.
sim.p1: This repository contains a real GitHub Copilot setup under .github/: a cheap project router, three specialists, area-scoped instructions, two skills and prompt templates.
sim.was.p1: Imagine: you ask GitHub Copilot in VS Code for a change to this project – just like asking a colleague for help. Behind the scenes, the agent team from the previous lesson gets to work: a router receives your request, picks the right specialist and loads rules and checklists for it.
sim.was.p2: The simulator plays exactly that through – without real AI, nothing is actually executed. Pick an example request below and follow the four steps: arrival → choice of specialist → loaded context → cost.
sim.f2: .github/instructions/*.instructions.md – area rules (applyTo), loaded only on matches
sim.f5: .github/prompts/*.prompt.md – saved request templates, invoked in chat via /name ('/new-lesson', '/explain')
sim.s1.titel: Change the colour of the active lesson
sim.s1.grund: CSS/design → @ui. Changes to the appearance need a strong coding model and edit tools.
sim.s2.grund: New lesson → @logic + skill 'new-lesson'. Registry, types and BOTH language files must stay consistent.
sim.s3.titel: Fix a typo in the README
sim.s3.grund: Text only, no code → @docs with a cheap model. No area rules needed.
sim.s4.grund: Verification procedure → @logic + skill 'i18n-check' (runs npm run check:i18n and interprets the result).
sim.s5.grund: Pure knowledge question, no file access needed. The router answers itself – no expensive model, no extra context.
sim.schritt1: Step 1 – arrival: your request first lands at the router 'project' (Claude Haiku 4.5 – small and cheap). It reads ONLY the request, no code yet.
sim.schritt1.agentmode: Step 1 – arrival: without a custom agent, agent mode handles the request directly – with the model from your picker and the full toolbox. Exactly which is not fixed.
sim.schritt1.askmode: Step 1 – arrival: ask mode takes your request as a conversation – it answers and explains, but does not touch the files itself.
sim.schritt3: Step 3 – what the specialist gets loaded into its context:
sim.schritt4: Step 4 – what is fixed – and what does it cost?
sim.ctrl.modell.builtin: uncertain – whatever is in the picker (maybe too expensive OR too weak)
sim.ctrl.tools.custom: only the necessary ones (set per role)
sim.keinagent: No delegation: the router answers the question itself – it doesn't get cheaper than this.
sim.wer.agentmode: Agent mode · model from the picker (not fixed)
sim.wer.askmode: Ask mode · model from the picker (not fixed)
sim.grund.agentmode: The built-in agent mode is universal – but NOTHING is fixed: it runs on the model from your picker (which may be too expensive OR too weak), has the full toolbox and no focus on the task.
sim.grund.askmode: Ask mode is ideal for questions and explanations. For actual file changes it is the wrong tool.
sim.beruehrte.keine: none – it is just a question
sim.files.ask: none – ask mode only reads, it changes nothing
sim.ctx.keine: only the base rules – this task needs nothing more
sim.tg.p: Experiment: what happens when a mechanism is missing? Switch it off and watch how warnings and costs change.
sim.at: Names with @ (e.g. @ui) are the roles from .github/agents/ – in the real Copilot chat you select or mention them exactly like this. You can also pick a specialist DIRECTLY at any time and skip the router – it is a convenience, not a requirement.
sim.warn.applyto: Without applyTo, all area rules must move into the always-on instructions – EVERY request gets more expensive.
sim.warn.skill: Without the skill the checklist is missing – high risk of forgetting a step (e.g. the EN keys!).
sim.warn.agentmode: In agent mode nothing is fixed: the model comes from the picker (may be too expensive OR too weak), the toolbox is full, there is no focus. A custom agent decides all of this deliberately.
sim.warn.askmode: Ask mode cannot edit files or run commands itself – it only explains the task. For actual changes you need agent mode or a custom agent.
sim.warn.keine: ✓ No warnings – a good fit for this request.
sim.tok.naiv: Naive setup (one agent, everything always loaded)
sim.tok.hinweis: Simplified cost points (tokens × model price: Haiku 1 · Sonnet 5 · Opus 10). With a built-in mode the model is uncertain – hence a range from the cheapest to the most expensive picker model.
sim.fazit: The real win of a custom agent is not 'cheaper' but FIXED: model, tools and focus are chosen deliberately – predictable and fitting. With a built-in mode you leave that to the picker: sometimes too expensive, sometimes too weak. Switch above and watch the fixed point turn into a range.
lektion.struktur.kurz: How a React app is put together – from boot to tree.
lektion.struktur.aufgabe: Trace the data flow in this app: open src/App.tsx and find out where `activeId` lives. Who READS the value? Who CHANGES it (three places: list, back, next)? You will find exactly this pattern – state up top, props down, events up – in every React app.
struct.h: How a React app is put together
struct.p1: Every React app starts the same way: index.html contains only an empty <div id="root">. In main.tsx, createRoot(...).render(<App />) says: 'React, take over this div and show the App component.' From then on the page belongs to React.
struct.p2: From App a TREE of components grows: App shows header, list and content; the content shows the current lesson; the lesson shows buttons and texts. Every component is a branch that can have branches of its own.
struct.p3: Data flows in ONE direction: props go top-down (parent → child), events go bottom-up via callback functions (child → parent). State lives where it is needed – when it changes, React re-renders only the affected part of the tree.
struct.p4: Re-rendering is cheap: React compares the new result with the old one (this is called reconciliation) and only touches what really changed in the browser.
struct.baum.hinweis: This is how the components of this project hang together:
struct.t.list: shows all lessons, reports clicks upwards
struct.f1: JSX – HTML-like syntax in the middle of JavaScript; { } inserts real code.
struct.f2: Props – values from parents to children; cleanly typed in TypeScript.
struct.f3: useState – a component's memory; changing it = re-rendering.
struct.f4: useEffect – reacting to things outside (loading data, timers). In depth in lesson 12.
struct.f5: useContext – shared values for the whole tree without a props chain (that is how the language switch works here).
struct.f6: .map() + key – turning data arrays into lists on screen.
struct.f7: Conditional rendering – { condition && <Element /> } shows something only when needed.
lektion.werkzeuge.kurz: Which libraries work here – and where to change what.
lektion.werkzeuge.aufgabe:
1) Open src/index.css and change the accent colour --accent (e.g. to #2563eb). Save – the whole app recolours.
2) Change the <title> in index.html and watch the browser tab.
3) Then reset everything with: git restore .  – that is exactly what the playground is for.
tools.p1: A React project is never React alone. These libraries and tools work together here – all of them are listed in package.json, npm install downloads them into node_modules:
tools.spalte.name: Tool
tools.lib.react: The UI library itself: components, props, state, hooks.
tools.lib.reactdom: Connects React to the browser: createRoot() mounts the app into the DOM (the real page).
tools.lib.vite: Dev server & bundler: starts the app in seconds, hot-reloads changes instantly and builds the final bundle (npm run build).
tools.lib.ts: JavaScript + types: mistakes show up while typing instead of in the browser.
tools.lib.oxlint: The linter: finds problematic patterns in the code (npm run lint).
tools.lib.reactlive: The live editor in the basics lessons: runs edited example code instantly in the browser (with prism-react-renderer for syntax highlighting).
tools.lib.node: The runtime and the package manager: npm run dev, npm install & co. run on top of them.
tools.nicht.p: No router (pages switch via state here), no server/fetch library, no CSS framework – the CSS is hand-written. That keeps visible what React itself does. These tools come in stage 3 (see the roadmap).
map.h: Map: what do I change where?
map.p1: The most common change wishes and their places:
map.g1: change a text or a translation
map.g3: change the look of individual parts
map.g5: change the order or groups of the lessons
map.g7: change the title in the browser tab
play.hinweis: Change the code – the preview below updates instantly. This is a sandbox: the real project files stay untouched, and 'Reset' restores the start at any time.
play.render: The last line render(...) decides what the preview shows.
lektion.bedingt.kurz: Showing something only when a condition holds.
lektion.bedingt.aufgabe: In the playground: 1) Add a second, secret paragraph that ONLY appears when logged out (using !loggedIn &&). 2) Replace the && expression with the ?: notation. Observe: both produce the same result.
bed.p1: In React you decide with plain JavaScript WHAT gets rendered. The two most important patterns: condition && <Element /> shows the element only when the condition is true. condition ? <A /> : <B /> shows either A or B.
bed.p2: You already know this from this app: the task box only appears when the lesson has a task (taskKey && ... in App.tsx).
lektion.listen.kurz: A data array becomes a list on screen.
lektion.listen.aufgabe: In the playground: 1) Add your own starting item to the shopping list. 2) Add an 'X' button per row that deletes the item – hint: setItems(items.filter(i => i !== item)). 3) Temporarily remove the key attribute and open the browser console (F12): React warns you.
li.p1:
In React, data almost always lives in arrays. With items.map(item =>
  • ...
    • ) you turn every element into a piece of UI – the list on screen automatically follows the data.
li.p2: Every list element needs a key attribute with a stable, unique value. That is how React recognises which element is which on re-render – otherwise the display can get mixed up.
li.p3: You know this one too: the lesson list on the left is built exactly like this (LessonList.tsx).
lektion.gemeinsam.kurz: Lifting state up so several components share it.
lektion.gemeinsam.aufgabe: In the playground: 1) Add a third <Display /> – all of them count in sync. 2) Add a second button 'Reset' that gets onClick={() => setCount(0)}. 3) Think about it: why can the state NOT live inside the button itself? (Answer: then the displays would know nothing about it.)
gem.h: Lifting state up: the state lives with the shared parent
gem.p1: When several components need to see the same value, the state moves into the CLOSEST SHARED PARENT component. From there it flows down as a prop; changes travel back up as callbacks.
gem.p2: That is exactly how this app works: activeId lives in App.tsx – the list reports clicks upwards, content and navigation read the value.
lektion.effekt.kurz: Reacting to the world outside: timers, data, cleanup.
lektion.effekt.aufgabe: In the playground: 1) Change the interval from 1000 to 100 milliseconds. 2) Temporarily remove the cleanup line (return () => clearInterval(id)) and press 'Reset' several times – the clock jumps erratically because old timers keep running. That is exactly what cleanup protects against! 3) Put the line back.
eff.p1: Rendering should do one thing only: turn data into display. Everything else – starting timers, loading data, registering event listeners – are 'side effects'. That is what useEffect is for: the code inside runs AFTER rendering.
eff.p2: The square bracket at the end controls WHEN the effect runs: [] = once after the first render, [value] = whenever value changes, no bracket = after every render.
eff.p3: If the effect returns a function, React calls it on cleanup (when the component disappears or the effect runs again). That way no timers or connections are left behind.
eff.ablauf.h: How the example runs, step by step
eff.ablauf.p: The code above goes through three phases. The key question is WHEN the effect runs – namely after rendering, and thanks to the empty list [] only a single time.
eff.ph1.s1: React calls the function Clock() for the first time.
eff.ph1.s2: useState(0) returns seconds = 0 and the setter function setSeconds.
eff.ph1.s3: useEffect(...) is called, but React merely remembers the effect – it is NOT executed yet.
eff.ph1.s4: The JSX is returned: "Diese Uhr läuft seit 0 Sekunden." appears on screen.
eff.ph1.s5: ONLY NOW does React run the effect function: setInterval starts the browser timer, its handle lands in the variable id.
eff.ph1.s6: The effect returns the cleanup function. React stores it – it is not called yet.
eff.ph2.s1: The browser calls the timer function: setSeconds((s) => s + 1).
eff.ph2.s2: React computes the new value – 0 becomes 1.
eff.ph2.s3: The state has changed, so React calls Clock() again.
eff.ph2.s4: useState(0) now returns 1! The 0 is only the starting value the very first time, not a reset.
eff.ph2.s5: useEffect is called again – but React compares the list [] with [] : unchanged, so the effect does NOT run again. The old timer simply keeps ticking.
eff.ph2.s6: React updates only the changed number in the browser, not the whole page.
eff.ph3.s1: You switch lessons or press "Reset" – the component disappears.
eff.ph3.s2: React calls the stored cleanup function: clearInterval(id) stops the timer.
eff.detail.h: Two details that explain the code
eff.d1.h: Why setSeconds((s) => s + 1) and not setSeconds(seconds + 1)?
eff.d1.p: The effect runs only once, on the first render – and there seconds is exactly 0. That value stays frozen inside the timer function forever (the term for this is a stale closure). So setSeconds(seconds + 1) would compute 0 + 1 forever and the clock would be stuck at 1. The form s => s + 1 instead asks React for the CURRENT value – which is why it counts up correctly.
eff.d2.p: Without clearInterval the timer keeps running even when the component is long gone. Every time it is shown again another timer is added – two timers make the counter jump in steps of two, three in steps of three. The reason you notice this immediately is StrictMode (see src/main.tsx): in development React runs effects twice on purpose – set up, clean up, set up again – precisely to expose missing cleanup.
eff.merksatz: Mnemonic: rendering = turning data into display. useEffect = everything after that which reaches outside. And whatever you start, you must also clean up.
mehr.p6: You can try the core principle of context right here – a mini example with a colour instead of a language:
lektion.mechanismen.kurz: Instructions, skills or agent – when do you use which?
lektion.mechanismen.aufgabe:
Match them up – where do these three new rules belong?
(a) "CSS colours always via the variables from index.css"
(b) "How to add a third language: 5 steps"
(c) "The test agent uses a cheap model and may only read"
Check your answers by looking into .github/ to see which folder fits. (Solution: a → instructions/, b → skills/, c → agents/ – (a) even exists there already.)
mech.h: Why three mechanisms – and not everything in one place?
mech.p1: At first glance it looks like duplication: there is an i18n instruction AND an i18n skill. The difference is not the topic but the TRIGGER – the three mechanisms are activated by completely different things and stay loaded for different lengths of time.
mech.k1.dauer: Loaded automatically as soon as a matching file is involved.
mech.k2.frage: What am I about to do?
mech.k2.dauer: On demand only – otherwise just the short description is visible.
mech.k3.dauer: For the whole session, whatever task comes along.
mech.i18n.p1: The instruction (i18n.instructions.md) holds RULES – what must always be true: both language files have the same keys, placeholders use single curly braces, a key is never renamed without its usages.
mech.i18n.p2: The skill (i18n-check/SKILL.md) holds a PROCEDURE – how to go about it: run check:i18n, then react depending on the message (PARITY, MISSING, UNUSED) and repeat until everything is green.
mech.i18n.p3: So they do not overlap in content. The instruction's last line ("afterwards run npm run check:i18n") is even a deliberate handover: the instruction says THAT you must verify – the skill says HOW to fix the result.
mech.f1.note: Instruction only: a language file is touched, so applyTo fires. The five-step diagnostic tree would be pure waste here.
mech.f2.titel: Check whether the translations are complete
mech.f2.note: Skill only: if everything is fine, no language file is opened at all – so applyTo may never fire. You still need the procedure.
mech.f3.note: Both: files in two areas are touched (rules) and at the end it gets verified (procedure).
mech.warum.h: Why not put everything into the agent file?
mech.w1: Lifetime: the agent file is loaded for the entire session. But @logic sometimes works purely on TypeScript types or on a script – then you pay for the i18n rules every time, with no benefit.
mech.w2: Duplication: i18n concerns TWO agents – @ui adds visible texts, @logic owns the JSON files. In agent files you would have to maintain the same rules twice, and in three months they will have drifted apart.
mech.w3: Instructions apply regardless of the agent – the strongest argument: they also fire when no agent is selected at all (just the model picker) or when someone addresses @ui directly. Agent content only applies while that particular agent is running. The parity rule, however, must ALWAYS hold.
mech.w4: Separation of concerns: the agent file answers 'who am I, which model, which tools'. Mixing file rules and procedures in there makes exactly the most expensive piece of context grow.
mech.baum.h: Rule of thumb: where does new knowledge belong?
mech.baum.p: When you add something, decide by WHAT IT DEPENDS ON:
mech.b1.frage: Applies to certain files, whenever they are touched
mech.b2.frage: Is a procedure with steps you only need sometimes
mech.b3.frage: Describes a role: model, tools, responsibility
mech.fazit: Honestly: for a project this size you could merge them. This setup separates them cleanly on purpose, because it is a teaching example. In a big repo with 20 rule areas it becomes a real advantage – which is exactly what the simulator in the next lesson shows you when you switch the applyTo toggle off.
lektion.shm.kurz: Making the agent more efficient (tokens) and more capable.
lektion.shm.aufgabe:
Open scripts/check-i18n.mjs and the skill .github/skills/i18n-check. Think about it: which steps would the model otherwise have to do itself – and how expensive (in tokens) would that be? (Hint: both JSON files together are ~700 lines.)
Bonus: open .github/hooks/hooks.json and scripts/pre-tool-guard.mjs – which file paths would Copilot's preToolUse guard deny?
shm.p1: A good agent setup does not stop at instructions, agents and skills. Three more building blocks make it more efficient (fewer tokens) and more capable (more abilities).
shm.skript.h: Helper scripts – doing deterministic work cheaply
shm.skript.p1: A script always does the same thing: same input → same result. The agent CALLS it instead of reasoning itself. That is exactly what saves tokens.
shm.skript.p2: Example from this project: npm run check:i18n (scripts/check-i18n.mjs). Without the script, the model would have to read both language files – ~700 lines together – in full and compare all keys in its head. That costs many thousands of tokens and is error-prone. With the script: one command, one result line.
shm.skript.vorher: Model compares all keys by hand
shm.skript.faustregel: Rule of thumb: is a task deterministic (always the same result)? Then make it a script – not model reasoning. This exact script is what the i18n-check skill calls.
shm.hook.p1: A hook is a command that GitHub Copilot runs automatically on an EVENT. Around an agent's tools the two most important events are preToolUse (right BEFORE a tool call – it can even DENY it) and postToolUse (right AFTER).
shm.hook.p2: The difference from an instruction is crucial: an instruction TELLS the model to do something – it can forget. A hook DOES it automatically – it cannot be forgotten and costs no model tokens.
shm.hook.p3: This repo has a real Copilot hook: .github/hooks/hooks.json wires up a preToolUse guard (scripts/pre-tool-guard.mjs). It runs BEFORE every file change and DENIES edits to generated files (e.g. dist/, package-lock.json). Copilot loads these hooks automatically for all agents in this repo (currently a preview feature in VS Code).
shm.hook.p4: Hooks come at two levels: repo-wide in .github/hooks/*.json (applies to all agents) or agent-scoped directly in an .agent.md. Example: .github/agents/logic.agent.md has a postToolUse hook that calls scripts/i18n-hook.mjs – it only checks whether de.json and en.json are in sync when the logic agent is working.
shm.hook.p5: Technically: the hook receives the tool call as JSON on standard input (incl. tool_name and tool_input.filePath) and answers with a JSON decision. A preToolUse hook can return "deny" and STOP the call; a postToolUse hook can only react (check, remind, log).
shm.hook.p6: The payoff: a hook enforces a rule automatically on EVERY tool call – the model can't forget it, it costs no model tokens, and with preToolUse a risky action can even be prevented BEFORE it happens.
shm.mcp.p1: MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. An MCP server is a small program that gives the agent NEW tools – e.g. access to a database, a ticket system, a web search or the file system.
shm.mcp.p2: Instead of building every tool yourself, you 'plug in' an MCP server. Its tools then appear in the agent's tools list (e.g. github/* for all tools of a GitHub server). That way the agent's capability grows without changing its base behaviour.
shm.mcp.p3: In short: scripts and hooks make the agent more EFFICIENT, MCP servers make it more CAPABLE.
shm.tab.h: The three building blocks at a glance
shm.tab.skript.zweck: saves tokens: deterministic work written once
